intro: Scarlatti sets pointed repeated gestures inside a three-beat measure. In Marcelle Meyer’s piano performance, follow how separated attacks and longer lines share the same pulse.
question: What holds the three-beat movement together when the gestures keep changing?

sections.label: First half
sections.mNote: three-beat gestures lead towards the dominant

sections.label: First half repeated
sections.mNote: opening route heard a second time

sections.label: Second half
sections.mNote: harmonic excursions lead back towards E major

sections.label: Second half repeated
sections.mNote: the return route is retraced before the close

cues.title: Three beats, pointed gestures
cues.text: Keep a three-beat pulse beneath the short repeated gestures. Scarlatti alternates articulated notes with more connected figures, so the phrase can change character without changing its metre.
cues.evidence: The inspected score is in 3/4 and juxtaposes reiterated notes with more flowing figures. The audio report does not reliably identify the beat; its 185-bpm estimate is not adopted as a tempo instruction. Score: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/7d/IMSLP691879-PMLP297350-keyboard_Sonata_in_E_major,_K.380.pdf
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A royal keyboard pupil
cues.text: Scarlatti enters Portuguese royal service in 1719 and teaches the Infanta Maria Bárbara. When her marriage takes her to Spain in 1729, he follows; their long musical association supplies the setting for much of his keyboard repertory.
cues.evidence: Cristina Fernandes, Treccani biography, documents the Portuguese appointment, royal teaching and move to Spain: https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/giuseppe-domenico-scarlatti_%28Dizionario-Biografico%29/

cues.title: Cadence and breathing space
cues.text: Towards the end of this first traversal, the line relaxes before the opening is heard again. Listen for the phrase’s release as well as its articulated notes: a repeat needs a recognisable ending to make its return clear.
cues.evidence: The score closes its first forty-bar half with a repeat sign. The report shows a level drop from −9.5 dB at 1:10 to −23.1 dB at 1:20, then a boundary at 1:24 and a renewed opening-like pitch profile. The precise repeat attack is not aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Compare the second traversal
cues.text: On the repeated first half, compare the balance between the upper line and the lower notes. The written route is familiar; the useful question is how the same gestures retain their shape when heard again.
cues.evidence: The repeated half is provisionally mapped from about 1:24 to 2:48. The report’s 0:34 and 1:58 boundaries and recurring pitch-class profiles support a repeated span; this does not claim a change in Meyer’s pedalling or articulation.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A copy is not composition
cues.text: The date 1754 belongs to the Venice manuscript copy of K. 380, not a securely dated act of composition. Scarlatti’s surviving sonatas depend heavily on manuscript collections; their order does not supply a simple chronology of invention.
cues.evidence: The existing Scarlatti biography identifies K. 380’s Venice-copy date. Treccani explains the copying of the Venice and Parma volumes and the absence of secure composition dates: https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/giuseppe-domenico-scarlatti_%28Dizionario-Biografico%29/

cues.title: The other half’s route
cues.text: The second half begins from the dominant region reached by the first. Its changing harmonies eventually bring the closing material home to E major. This is a two-part design with repeats, not a miniature version of a later four-movement sonata.
cues.evidence: The score’s double bar after bar 40 separates two repeated halves; the second begins in the B-major region and closes in E. The 2:48–3:20 measured changes support this broad placement, not the timing of each modulation.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The bass sets direction
cues.text: Through the return towards E major, follow the lower part beneath the melody’s decorations. Repeated upper notes can sound stable while a moving bass changes their harmonic meaning.
cues.evidence: The score’s second half places decorated upper figures over changing lower notes. This is a passage-level listening invitation; the analysis does not isolate the pianist’s hands or identify a particular inversion at 3:36.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Beyond the keyboard sonatas
cues.text: Scarlatti’s earlier employment includes opera and sacred music in Rome. Before the Iberian courts and their keyboard collections, he works for the exiled Polish queen Maria Casimira and then directs the Cappella Giulia at St Peter’s.
cues.evidence: Treccani documents the Roman operas for Maria Casimira and Scarlatti’s succession to Tommaso Baj at the Cappella Giulia in 1714: https://www.treccani.it/enciclopedia/giuseppe-domenico-scarlatti_%28Dizionario-Biografico%29/

cues.title: Recognition without a new theme
cues.text: During the repeated second half, recognise the route rather than waiting for another theme. The closing gestures acquire their final purpose by reaching E major, the home key that the first half left behind.
cues.evidence: The second-half repeat is estimated from the quiet span near 4:00 followed by the level renewal at 4:05. Similar changes at 3:08 and 4:26 support retracing the later material; this is not bar alignment.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The sound after the close
cues.text: The final phrase releases into the piano’s remaining resonance. Listen for the difference between the ending of the musical pattern and the disappearance of the recorded sound.
cues.evidence: The report falls from −18.1 dB at 5:15 to −27.5 dB at 5:20 and −54.0 dB at 5:25, with no detected attacks in the last two windows. The minor-key labels during the decay are not treated as a change of ending.

transitions.title: A cadence sends us back
transitions.how: The first half reaches B major, the dominant of E. Its repeat sign then sends the player back to the opening instead of onwards to new material. The release at the cadence separates the two traversals; the returning rhythmic gestures make the larger repetition recognisable.
transitions.evidence: The score’s first repeat closes at bar 40. The level trough around 1:20 and boundary at 1:24 precede the return of the opening-like profile; 1:24 is an approximate map point.

transitions.title: The dominant becomes a starting point
transitions.how: After the first half has repeated, Scarlatti continues from its B-major destination into the second half. Familiar repeated and decorated gestures now support a different harmonic route. The eventual goal is the home tonic, E major, rather than another close in the dominant.
transitions.evidence: The written second half follows bar 40. The report’s 2:48 boundary and renewed level at 2:50 fit the large-scale division; the changing estimates after 2:55 are not used to name every chord.

transitions.title: The homeward route is retraced
transitions.how: The second half reaches E major, then repeats from its own beginning rather than from the beginning of the sonata. The listener therefore hears the departure from the dominant and the return home twice. Cadential release and renewed rhythmic attack make the repeat audible without a linking passage.
transitions.evidence: The score marks a repeat of the second half. The report shows a trough at 4:00 and a sharp renewal at 4:05, with later features recurring about seventy-eight seconds apart. The 4:04 boundary remains provisional.

fields.label: Performers
fields.note: Both recording sources identify Meyer; the chronology identifies the Scarlatti piano session. No historical keyboard type is inferred from the composition’s age.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Solo piano performance of the keyboard sonata
fields.note: A single complete sonata is hosted, not a movement from a multi-movement set. The date 1754 is retained as a Venice-manuscript copy date, not a proven composition date. Meyer’s edition and editorial interventions are unknown. The Longo reference score’s fingering, dynamics and other editorial directions are not attributed to Scarlatti or to Meyer. The two repeated halves are mapped provisionally from the score and audio report, not a note-by-note alignment.

facts: Son of the opera composer Alessandro Scarlatti; born in the same year as Bach and Handel
Naples and Rome; Portuguese royal service from 1719; followed Maria Bárbara to Spain in 1729
555 keyboard sonatas in Ralph Kirkpatrick’s catalogue; earlier operas, cantatas and sacred music
composer.background:
Domenico Scarlatti was born in Naples, the sixth child of Alessandro Scarlatti, an established composer of opera and sacred music. He entered professional musical life as a teenager, working as an organist and composing for the stage. Domenico eventually concentrated on keyboard music in courts far from Naples, taking a different path from his father’s large operatic career. His first decades included church appointments, singers, theatrical commissions and the practical education of a musician expected to supply whatever his employer required.

In Rome he worked for the exiled Polish queen Maria Casimira and at St Peter’s, writing both opera and sacred music. The ten-part Stabat Mater, usually associated with these Roman years, combines four soprano lines with pairs of altos, tenors and basses. Its voices enter in changing combinations, and the density of the counterpoint can contract around a particular text.
composer.epithet: An Italian court musician in Lisbon and Madrid who made keyboard sonatas out of hand crossings, repeated notes and abrupt changes of harmonic ground.
